prompt: Write an email to a colleague about how the falling cost of making things might change why people work. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the email only.
final_message:
Subject: Will cheaper making change why we work?

Hi Sam,

I've been thinking about something since our conversation last week, and I wanted to get it down while it's fresh. If the cost of making things keeps falling, what happens to the reasons people work?

For most of history, work has been tied closely to production. We worked because things were hard to make, and someone had to do the making. As software, design, writing, and even physical prototyping get cheaper, that link starts to loosen. A single person can now build what once took a team. That changes who gets to be a maker, and it changes what is scarce.

My rough view is that three motivations will shift in importance.

First, income. If goods and services get cheaper, the pay needed for a comfortable life could drop, at least in some categories. That doesn't mean jobs disappear, but it may mean fewer people feel they must take any job just to get by. Housing, healthcare, and education are the obvious exceptions, since they haven't followed the same cost curve. Whether those stay expensive may decide how much freedom the rest of this actually creates.

Second, judgment and taste. When anyone can produce a competent draft, a prototype, or a product, the bottleneck moves to deciding what is worth making. Knowing what people need, what's good, and what to leave out becomes the valuable part. I expect people to work more out of a sense of authorship and less out of obligation to execute.

Third, meaning and belonging. Work has always given people structure, status, and community, not just a paycheck. If production needs fewer hands, we'll have to be honest about how much of what people value in work is the social part. Some will find that in building small businesses, creative projects, or local services. Others may feel adrift, and I don't think we should wave that away.

There's also a risk worth naming. Cheap production can flood the world with mediocre output, which makes attention and trust the scarce resources. Work may shift toward curation, verification, and relationships, which are harder to automate and harder to scale.

I'm not predicting a tidy outcome. The benefits depend on how widely cheaper production is shared, and on whether institutions adapt as quickly as the technology does. But I do think the question "why do people work?" will be asked more openly than it has been in a long time.

I'd love your take, especially on whether you think the meaning piece is overstated. Do you have time for coffee next week?

Best,
